utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Registrar, could you call the case number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Jadranko Prlic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Madam Registrar. I'd like to greet everyone in the courtroom, members of the Prosecution, Defence counsel, and the accused. The Chamber will now render two oral decisions. The first one which I will read out slowly is as follows: The oral decision of the Chamber concerning the Praljak motion for the admission into evidence of documents relating to Mr. Josip Manolic. The accused Praljak filed a motion on the 27th of November, 2006, in which four documents were requested to be admitted into evidence, documents shown to the witness Josip Manolic on the 5th of July, 2006. The numbers are 3D 00313, 3D 00314, 3D 00320, and 3D 00186. The Chamber would first of all like to point out that, although the witness Manolic appeared before the Chamber on the 3rd, 4th, 5th and 6th of July, 2006, it is necessary to implement the decision of the 13th of July, 2006, that concerns the admission of documents into evidence. With regard to 3D 00313, document 3D 00313, and 3D 00314, the Chamber notes that the witness was not in a position to enlighten the Chamber with regard to the authenticity and probative value or relevance of this document. With regard to 3D 00320, the Chamber notes that this document was not shown to the witness Josip Manolic. As far as document 3D 00186 is concerned, the Chamber first of all notes that the witness Josip Manolic did not enlighten the Chamber with regard to the authenticity, probative value or relevance of this document. However, this same document was subsequently shown to the witness Peter Galbraith, and the document was admitted into evidence on the 27th of September, 2006. And as a result, the Trial Chamber hereby decides not to admit into evidence 3D 00313, 3D 00314. I'll repeat that. The Trial Chamber hereby decides not to admit 3D 00313, 3D 00314, and 3D 00320. And the Trial Chamber notes that it is not necessary for Praljak, the accused Praljak, to demand the 3D 00186 be admitted into evidence since this document has already been admitted into evidence. And now for the second oral decision that concerns the admission of documents into evidence that relate to Witness CA, who appeared on the 13th of November, 2006. The Trial Chamber will now decide on the admission of documents into evidence, documents that relate to the witness CA, who appeared on the 13th of November, 2006. The Chamber hereby decides to admit the following documents into evidence. These documents were presented by the Prosecution, and this decision is being rendered since the documents have a certain probative value and a certain relevance: P 02009, P 02191, P 02200. In addition, the Trial Chamber has to decide on P 02063. The Chamber has to decide on whether to admit this document into evidence. The authenticity of this document has been contested by the Stojic Defence. The Stojic Defence claimed that the signature on the contested document wasn't the signature of Marko Rozic, who allegedly signed the document. In support of its argument, the Stojic Defence, first of all, presented a document for comparison, 3D 00563, signed by Marko Rozic. In addition, Defence counsel claimed that this person could not have signed the contested document since he was in -- in detention when the contested document was drafted, which was on the 23rd of April, 1993. To respond to this -- to respond to this objection, the Prosecution filed, on the 21st of November, 2006, three documents from the archives of the Republic of Croatia and from the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the contents of which are identical to the contents of document P 02063. It is the Trial Chamber's opinion that the signature on document P 02063 is the signature of the same individual as the signature on the document used for comparison, document 3D 00563. In addition, the Trial Chamber is of the opinion that the fact that Marko Rozic was in detention for a few hours on the 23rd of April, 1993, does not exclude the possibility of him signing this document later on that day. And finally, the other indicia in support of the authenticity of the contested document, other indicia such as the stamp and the number under which it was recorded. The Chamber hereby decides, therefore, to admit into evidence P 02063 as it has a certain probative value and a certain relevance. The Chamber would also like to point out that the Defence teams have not requested that documents be admitted into evidence in relation to the testimony of Witness CA. We'll now move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, we are in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now that we're in open session, I will give the floor to the Prosecution so that they can make their summary.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, and good afternoon to everyone in the courtroom. The brief summary of this witness goes as follows: This witness was living with her family in the village of Bivolje Brdo, municipality of Capljina, until July 1993. The witness's husband was a member of a Muslim unit within the HVO. On the night of the 30th of June, 1st of July, 1993, most of his unit was arrested by the HVO on the front line. The witness's husband was not arrested because he was on leave. On the 1st of July, a group of 30 HVO soldiers arrived in Bivolje Brdo and searched the houses and mistreated the women to find out where the men were hiding. The witness was threatened. During the next few days, the soldiers kept coming to look for the witness's husband and for any hidden weapons. On each occasion, they ill-treated the witness and her neighbours. In the evening of the 13th of July, 1993, the witness, together with part of her family, fled her village as she was told the HVO were shelling the area. They fled towards Lokva and were fired upon by HVO. In the morning of 13th July, 1993, the witness was told that Lokva was in flames. When the witness got to Lokva in the evening, the village was empty. The witness spent the night in the woods with villagers from Lokva who had fled in the morning. There were at least 500 villagers from Bivolje Brdo. On the 14th of July, the witness was arrested by HVO soldiers and taken with other civilians to the Silos in Capljina. There was a check point at the entry of the Silos where the belongings of the witness and the other Muslim civilians were searched. They were crammed into a room without a ceiling. There were at least 150. The witness had a baby with her and could hardly move. They received nothing for food, had only a bucket for a toilet. Around the 15th of July, the witness and others were transferred to Gradina in trucks, where she stayed for about eight days. Around the 23rd of July, she and others were transferred to Sovici, stayed in the primary school for one night, and were then taken to Doljani by truck where they were told to walk towards --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honours, this summary is not accurate as far as we can see. When -- we don't know where it comes from. It seems to contain information which we've not seen before. We have commented before. We did suggest that summaries might be supplied to us in advance to avoid this sort of problem. It would be a good idea if we are now going to discuss this, it would probably be better if the witness were not here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Madam Egels, normally the summary should follow the 92 ter summary. Now, if there are any new elements with respect to -- 65 ter, interpreter's correction. Then it is your duty to inform the Defence thereof, of the new elements. Mr. Stewart is telling us that there are new elements. Now, I myself don't know which they are because I don't have the 65 ter summary to check that out. So is Mr. Stewart wrong or right? You -- is it you who are in the right or Mr. Stewart? Can you respond to Mr. Stewart's objection? He says that there are new elements with respect to the 65 ter summary.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: I was just going to ask my colleague which new elements he was referring to, because, to my knowledge, this summary is a summary of the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm slightly reluctant to do that with the witness here, Your Honour. This isn't a debate which should take place in the witness's hearing. It's only fair to her, the witness, that it doesn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but, Mr. Stewart, the time it takes to have the witness shown out of the courtroom and back in we're going to lose precious time. So either what you say is well grounded or --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... procedures we had suggested for practical purposes. I really do not know why our suggestion that the summary should be supplied in advance was not adopted. As an obvious piece of common sense, I specifically suggested it so that it would save this sort of waste of time. But, Your Honour, all right. What happened on the way to Lokva, shooting and so on, we don't see that anywhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis, two points. Mr. Stewart is quite right in the extent to which he says that it would be advisable for the summary read out in the courtroom should be provided to the Defence in advance. That is the least that the Prosecution can do. Now, why wasn't that, in fact, done, Mr. Mundis?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, as we've indicated in the past, the summaries are generally based upon the 65 ter summaries. I can't answer the specific question concerning this witness. Let me consult with my colleagues and perhaps the process that we'll adopt is simply to read the 65 ter summary into the record to avoid this kind of problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I think that would be the best way to go about it. Please continue, Ms. Egels.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: Just to answer the issue of the firing upon, it can be found in paragraph one, two, three, four, five -- paragraph number 6 on page 10 of the statement of this witness. So just to finish on that summary. Around the 23rd of July, they were transferred to Sovici, stayed in the primary school for one night, and were then taken to Doljani by truck, where they were told to walk in the direction indicated by the HVO soldiers in order to reach the Bosnian front line from where they were taken to Jablanica.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness CG. You provided a written statement to investigators of the Office of the Prosecutor of the ICTY in February and March of 2001; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: Did you provide this statement freely?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: When you answered to the questions of the investigator, did you answer truthfully?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: At the end of the interview, was your statement read back to you in your own language?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: Did you sign that statement in the French language? And maybe I can ask the witness to look at Exhibit number 9770, which is in front of her. At the bottom of this page, is this your signature?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: Yesterday, when you met with me and an investigator, you were given the opportunity to review your statement in your own language; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: Upon reviewing your statement in your own language, you had some corrections to make; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: Is it correct that on page 3, paragraph 12 of the English version of your statement, which is page 3, paragraph 7 of the French version, when it says the Serbian house which had been abandoned, that that sentence should be deleted and should be replaced by the sentence: "The Serbian house first floor was used as a school and the upper floor as an apartment by a Serbian family until it was shelled by the Serbs"? Is that what you told us yesterday?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: On page 9, paragraph 6 of the English version of your statement, which is page 7, paragraph 4 of the French version of your statement, you wanted to correct the sentence which said that: "They made me responsible for going and finding out because there was an arms cache." And you wanted to explain that you were the one who offered to go and check what had happened to the village of Bucevici; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: And finally on page 10, paragraph 5 of the English version of your staple, which is page 7, paragraph 11 of the French version, when it is referred to a certain -- and maybe we can go into private session, Your Honour, because I will have to name a person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: Witness, should you be asked today to provide a full statement to this Court, would the content of that testimony be the same as what is in your written statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: I would like to show you some documents now, Witness CG. Can I ask you to go to Exhibit number 3035. This -- in your statement, you mentioned the arrest of all the men in your husband's unit during the night of 30 June to 1st of July, 1993. This document is an order by a commander, Ivan Primorac, dated the 30th of June, 1993. I would like you to take a look at items 6 and 9 of that order. And this is on page 2 of the version in your language and on page 1 of the English version.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, with your permission, before the witness answers that question, I should like us to clarify the previous question, whether the 3rd Brigade of the HVO was active in the area in which the witness lived and resided, or was it the 3rd Brigade of the HVO, whose order this is, was in some other territory? Because if it was active in some other territory, then there are no grounds for this witness to comment on this particular order. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Madam Egels.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: Yes, this is not part of my question, Your Honour, so would you like -- would you like me to ask that question, or do you think this is a question for cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You just wish to establish whether the contents of this document corresponds to the situation as she knew it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's the object of the exercise.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: Of course. I didn't even ask a question yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ask your question, then, and we'll see.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: So my question is: Paragraph 6 and 9 that I was referring to, do they correspond to what you experienced or perceived on the ground on that date?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: Can I now ask you to move to Exhibit number 3063, please. In your statement you mention that between the 1st of July and the 13th of July, 1993, HVO soldiers came on various occasions to your village to find out where the men were and if weapons were hidden. This document is an order by --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'd just like to draw your attention to the fact that this order is an order from another brigade, the 1st Brigade of the HVO, Knez Domagoj Brigade. So we really must ask the question of which of these brigades was active on the territory that the witness was on. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But the witness might not know who was on the ground. Ms. Egels, could you ask the witness whether she knew whether the 1st Brigade of the HVO was in the region. But, Counsel Alaburic, we're wasting time here. It's a useless exercise. But I don't want you to have the impression that we're not listening to what you are saying, so we'll ask Ms. Egels to ask her question. Ms. Alaburic, when you have a witness, your witness, called by you, who is faced with the same document and the Prosecution says but this witness knows nothing about that, you're going to be in the same situation. You're going to face exactly the same situation. So, Ms. Egels, ask the witness whether she knows of the existence of the 1st HVO Brigade in the area.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: Witness CG, do you know whether the 1st HVO Brigade, Knez Domagoj, was active in your area, in the area of Bivolje Brdo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I think that my husband was a member of the that brigade, the Knez Domagoj Brigade. I don't know what company and battalion he was in, but I think they held control of that territory and that they belonged to that same battalion, unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness CG. So to go back to this order, this is an order by commander Nedjelko Obradovic dated on the 1st of July, 1993, and I would like you to take a look at the first item of the order which is on page 1 of the version in your language and the English version. And I would like to know what this paragraph states about the mopping up of Bivolje Brdo. Does this correspond to what you experienced or perceived on the ground during those days?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it does correspond to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: Witness, can I ask you now to go to document number 3668, 3668. In your statement you mention that towards the end of July, 1993, you were taken together with other civilians from Gradina to Capljina, then to Risovac and then to the Sovici primary school in the middle of night where you were counted to be about 420 people. The first question is: Do you remember if on that journey you drove through the neighbourhood of Posusje?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: I would like you now to take a look at this document, number 3668, which is a handwritten draft request from the president of the HVO in Jablanica and an HVO commander, to amongst others, Valentin Coric and Berislav Pusic. And I would like to ask you if what is described in this text is conformed to what you experienced or is it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: Can I ask you now to go to Exhibit number 3652. Following up on that journey which brought you to the Sovici primary school. In your statement you say that you stayed a few hours after arriving in Sovici and that then you were taken by truck to Doljani where you were made to walk towards the ABiH line. I would like you to take a look at this document, which is a telex from Berislav Pusic to Jablanica, and I would like you to tell us if what is described in this text is conformed to what you experienced.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: Your Honours, if the Defence have no objection, I would like to tender also the following document, number 3665, which is in fact the implementation on the ground of the previous order, 3652. Otherwise, I'll show it to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: No objections from this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: Witness, can I ask you now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Counsel Tomasevic. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] We do have an objection, for the simple reason that this is an order pursuant to a order. We don't have the previous order. We don't have the signature to this order. We can't see who issued it or a stamp. All it says is what we see here. I don't know what we can deduce and prove based on an order, based on a previous order, which we haven't seen. So we object in principle. The authenticity of the document. There's no signature, no stamp. We haven't seen a single document like this. Documents are usually at least signed. We can't see who issued this, pursuant to whose orders. The military police department of a previous order of theirs, and I think we ought to be shown the previous document so that we can assess this one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're going to take note of your objection. Continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: So, Witness, Exhibit number 8858, please. And if I can ask you to go to the last page of this document which is page number 12 in both your language and the English version.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if we might go to private session because I will have to name names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Egels, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: Witness, can I ask you to go now to Exhibit number 9086. Do you recognise this place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court what this place is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's the Silo.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: Is this the place where you have been detained?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Egels, there are a number of photographs it seems. So are you going to ask the witness about all the photographs? If you're going to ask about all the photographs, then you have to give the numbers, 9943, 994, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: I was going to do that, Your Honour. I was just going to ask her to turn to number --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... 9739.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: 9739, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute. Ms. Egels, in the document 9086, there are a number of photographs: One, two, three, four. There are four. And each have a number, 9943, 9944, 9945, and 9946. Now, if you want to admit and tender the four photographs, then the witness will have to say, "I recognise 43. I recognise 44," et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: Your Honour, you're completely right. I was jumping already to the next one.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: Can I ask you to go back, please, to 9086, Exhibit 9086. And flip through all the photographs under that number and tell us if you recognise them. So the second -- the second photograph will be 0144-9944 at the bottom. Do you recognise this place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. This is also the Silo.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: Can you be more --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We would go out to relieve ourselves there while we were in detention and walk around a bit.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: And the next picture.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is also the Silo.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: For the record, this is the picture with -- at the bottom 0144-9945. The next one, please. And this is 0144-9946 at the bottom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. This is also the Silo.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: And the last picture of that exhibit number, which is 0144-9947 at the bottom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Also the Silo.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness CG. Can I ask you now to go to Exhibit number 9739. Do you recognise the place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the Silo.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: And number 9740?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's also the Silo.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: Can I ask you now to turn to number 9742.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is Bivolje Brdo.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: Can your house be seen from here, from that picture?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: Thank you. Number 9743, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the mine at Bivolje Brdo, and that's where the people killed were exhumed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: How do you know this place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I lived there, and we have a field nearby, and we went to watch it all when they were exhumed. And we went to the place afterwards as well, to visit it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: Finally, can I ask you to take a look at Exhibit number 9738. Do you recognise this place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do. This is the place we were in Sovici. I think it's the primary school in Sovici.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness CG.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no further exhibits to show to the witness and no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Counsel Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with your permission, before we start the cross-examination, I'd like to make two observations which I would like to be recorded in the transcript. My colleague from the Prosecution, when asking a question about Exhibit P 03668, and this was recorded on page 18, probably presented by mistake the erroneous assertion that the document was issued by the commander of the HVO of Jablanica whereas it was the president of the HVO of Jablanica who issued the document. And the second remark, with respect to my objections to the documents of the two different brigades, did not relate to the fact that I would expect the witness to speak to the authenticity of the document, but was along the lines that the witness can not tell us whether this was an order pursuant to an order if the order did not come from the territory and area she lived in. That was the gist of my objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Egels.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Just to set the record straight. On page -- let me check. Page 18, line 17 -- 16, 17, and 18, I said it was a draft request from the HVO in Jablanica and an HVO commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was what I was saying. It wasn't a commander, it was the president of the HVO, and this is an important difference. The president of the HVO represents civilian authorities, and the HVO commander represents military authority. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The Chamber will rule on the objections raised with regard to the admissibility of this document. It's now quarter past 3.00. We have half an hour before the break. The Defence has about an hour and a half in total. I don't know what you have agreed on. Mr. Karnavas, any questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I have no questions, but my time has been donated to the Praljak team.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Nozica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I apologise to Ms. Nozica that I take your time. I just want to come back to that exchange of views concerning what Ms. Egels said. And I believe that she said in lines 17, 19, that I said it and I now repeat and quote, "I said it was a draft request from the HVO in Jablanica and an HVO commander." So I believe that, for the record, it should be said that it was what she said and she didn't speak about the president or -- president of HVO in Jablanica. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas has given his 15 minutes to the Praljak Defence. An hour and a half. That's 45 minutes. That means 15 minutes for each Defence team. Ms. Nozica.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Mr. Praljak will start, and then I will follow on. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Praljak, you have 30 minutes; your 15 minutes plus the 15 minutes from the Prlic team. You have 30 minutes. Please go ahead. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Thank you. Cross-examination by the Accused Praljak:

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, madam. I can't use your name, so I'll just call you madam.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: I'll be dealing with 1992 and part of 1993. According to your statement, is it correct to say that the Serbian forces, the JNA, arrived in the area of Stolac, Mostar, the left bank, in the spring of 1992 and even earlier, but for you it was in March, 1993?

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: 1992. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: Is it correct to say, according to your statement, that at one point in time, we can't be precise, you and other people from your village fled to the right bank and went to Capljina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: And before, you were sheltered in the basement of a Croat's house, or all of you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: Do you know that at the time, in the area of Sevas Njive, a group of HVO soldiers transferred towards a hill, about 200 of them, and in April 1992, there were fierce clashes and there were people who were killed and wounded? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the time, I was in the shelter with my children, so I can't really say anything with certainty about that event.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: Thank you. After you had returned, there was the JNA. Things were still functioning to a certain extent, but reserve forces from Montenegro arrived at one point in time and the situation became extremely difficult and once again you and other people crossed the Neretva to the right bank; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: On the third page of the B/C/S version of your statement, you said that at the time they were trying to stop the JNA, trenches were dug in the vicinity of a house.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: And you said, "I think that these were HV soldiers." So soldiers from the Croatian army. And then you say, "Because at that time the HVO had not yet been established." Are you aware of the fact that at the time the HVO, regardless of whether this was official or not, already had units, people in Western Herzegovina had organised themselves, and is it correct to say that you personally saw any HVO soldiers with HVO insignia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw soldiers, but I didn't see any insignia, not exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Here you say, "We then left the shelter and went to a house behind a hill. This house belonged to Karlo Prce, a Croat." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: And then you go on to say that the intensive shelling continued. Normal life had been disrupted. Panic spread and we all fled to Pocitelj. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: And can we therefore conclude that there was fighting and the reserve forces from Serbia had attacked Capljina and they had taken the entire left bank of the Neretva. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I don't know exactly what they had taken, but I do know that there was panic in our village. There was shelling and my child had a wound in -- in her mouth, and I know it was like that in Bivolje Brdo. I don't know what it was like in Mostar and Capljina.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: I'm talking about Bivolje Brdo, in that area, not about Mostar. Thank you. I'm interested in another sentence of yours. Here you say, "When the Serbs started opening fire on the HV soldiers, soldiers who were digging trenches, well, they fled and they looted houses." A minute ago you said you didn't see these soldiers were Croatian soldier. How did you see them looting houses? Had you left earlier on? Were you in the basement? Or is this something you heard after the event?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't hear about that. But when we were returning home, things had been looted from our house.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: That's quite certain, but you go on to say, I'll find the passage. You said that, after the event, the Serbs, when you first returned there, you said your houses were looted. They had stolen your -- they had stolen your television and other electrical appliances; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: So we can conclude that you knew that the houses had been looted and when you return the second time, you knew that the Serbs had done that, but you didn't see the HVO and you don't know who exactly looted those houses, at least in relation to the HVO. Can you claim for sure that the HVO, at that time, looted your houses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't claim that with certainty, but my husband's mother didn't leave. She immediately returned home after the shelling and she was there throughout that period of time.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: Thank you. You know that the HVO -- or do you know that in June an HVO offensive in the direction of Stolac was started. Your husband participated in it and an area was liberated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: You say that, in Pocitelj, a mass of people gathered and then you crossed over to the other side in boat -- in a boat and there were lorries waiting to take you away. Do you know that on that occasion 10.000 people crossed the river over, some at a point near Pocitelj and others at Sevas Polje?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: Do you know that over 3.000 cars, used by the people to flee in, were in the area of Sevas Polje and Pocitelj. They were by the road, on the road, in the fields, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: Do you know that from the 13th, 14th, and 15th, 16th, and 17th of April, 1992, cars and even lorries were taken from the left bank of the Neretva to the right bank?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, to large extent.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: To a large extent. Do you know that even later, after the 17th of April and right up until the 20th, people came from Stolac, from Visoravan and crossed the Neretva, went to the right bank and went to shelters. Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: Do you know that I was the commander at the time. I was the commander down there and people were following my orders and my instructions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I think that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Let's show 3D 00595 to the witness, please. This is a report dated October 1992 signed by --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Usher, could you help the witness. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] 3D 00595.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: It's been signed by seven individuals. I'll read out the names. Tell me whether you know any of them. Zulfo Sabanovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: Mustafa Sabanovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: Enver Bojcic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I know Enver.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: Huseir Sabanovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Pardon.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: Huseir Sabanovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: Hamic Sabanovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: Dzafer Sabanovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: Sulejman Sabanovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: Thank you very much. This is a voluminous document. It relates to that period of time. Let's have a look at page 7 in the B/C/S version. Have a look at the second paragraph. On the 4th of April, 1992 -- it's on page 7, paragraph two. Have you found that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: It says: "From the right bank to the left bank of the Neretva, a unit with a hundred individuals crossed over with all their equipment." And then it says: "These people were escorted another unit in boats, a unit of about 60 people. And then on the third night, a group of about 50 individuals were taken across. They went to fight in Bivolje Brdo." And on page 8, paragraph three says: "On the 10th of April, fierce fighting broke out at the front in Bivolje Brdo. A tank unit set off from Pijesak in the direction of Bivolje Brdo. Artillery fire was opened. It was hell on Bivolje Brdo on that day. And also in Sevas Polje." And then the third paragraph, on the bottom of the same page, it says: "On this day in Bivolje Brdo, Beno Franjo died, Beno Martin as well, Raguz Dragan. There were others who were wounded," et cetera. Can you see that? Do you know anything about this, since that was near you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I heard about this, but at the time, I don't think I was at home.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: Thank you. You've heard about that. Now have a look at page 9. Towards the bottom of that page it says: "The entire column returned to Pocitelj and Sevas Polje. Vehicles were left, abandoned, and they crossed over the Neretva. The Crisis Staff assessed that at the time there were about 10.000 individuals in Pocitelj and Sevas Polje. The boats kept taking people across the Neretva," et cetera, et cetera. And then on page 10 there's a list. Have a look at page 10, please. It says, "On the 13th of April, the Chetniks attacked Capljina." Are you aware of the fact that at the time Capljina was shelled on a daily basis?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: Do you know that they were doing this from the left bank of the Neretva?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: And do you know that on the right bank, behind Capljina, in the village of Grabovina, that there was a barracks that belonged to the JNA. And they also opened fire on Capljina from there. Capljina was fired on from two directions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know that there was a barracks there because I was born in the vicinity, but I don't know whether there was shooting from it because I wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Then paragraph 4, it says, "On the 17th of April, all the refugees were taken across the Neretva River to Sevas Polje. Many vehicles were abandoned. In our assessment, there were about 3.000 of them." You have testified about this and that's correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: And then it goes on to say, and you've already testified about this, it says, "that all those vehicles were taken across as well as a lot of quite heavy lorries." Let's go on. Let's move on. Do you know that all these people were put up in houses in Medjugorje? They were put up in the complex that belonged to the Kompas company. They were put up in student homes in Capljina, in Ljubuski, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: So everybody was provided accommodation and was taken care of. Do you know if anyone went hungry?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: Thank you. And subsequently, as you yourself say, and that's what it also says in this document, units were established in which there were Muslims, and there was a company that was formed in Medjugorje as well as in Ljubuski?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I know that. A husband -- my husband was in one of those units.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: Did your husband ever say that he had met me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that these units were also trained?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: Thank you do you know that they were provided with weapons, equipment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: And in your statement, you say, "My husband organised a massive exodus of the people"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: You say there were lorries waiting there, et cetera. I don't doubt that. And here it says that many Muslims became involved and so on and so forth. But can you assess how many lorries, buses, and petrol was used, how many tyres were used to make a raft so that the lorries could be transported across the river, 3.000 vehicles, 12.000 people? Can you imagine the effort involvement.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, an immense effort.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And you also know that there was fierce fighting, Capljina was being shelled, it was burning around Mostar and so on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And then you go on to say that when you first returned, a gentleman approached you, his name was Sulejman Budakovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: Do you know that this gentleman, shortly after that event, shortly after that period, became the deputy commander of the ABiH 4th Corps in Mostar? He didn't immediately become the commander of the 4th Corps because there was no such unit but he became the commander of the headquarters of the ABiH in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know that he had some sort of official position, but I don't know of what kind.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: Madam, it's very simple. If you don't know, just say you don't know. None of us know everything here. And what I'm interested in is this, just a few more questions and then we'll be able to wind up. So the companies were formed, and those Muslim refugees were put up in the area, and afterwards, the following things happened: A large number of Muslims joined up with the HVO and another portion joined the Bregava Brigade that was established to the left of your village; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What I know is that many Muslims joined the HVO. Perhaps I heard about the rest of it, but I'm not quite sure, so I can't say.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: Tell me, please, did your husband receive a salary in the HVO just like the others, if they received a salary?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: You say at one place that you were forced to take Croatian dinars. Tell me, please, when you went shopping to the shops that were open, could you pay with German marks, if you had German marks of course?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we could.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: Could you pay in dollars, for example, if you happened to have dollars?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we could.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: Could you pay in French francs, if there were any around?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: So apart from those currencies, was there any other currency, except for the Croatian dinar, the currencies I've just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: You don't remember. Right. While your husband was in the HVO, up until that June or the end of June, 1993, did he happen to tell you that there was any -- ever any difference within the HVO in terms of weaponry, food, salaries, between Muslims and Croats, any differentiation there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: So they received equal treatment with regard to their shifts, going up to the front line and generally speaking?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: So you at the time as a civilian, you or your neighbours, could you go to Croatia, to Ploce, Metkovici, Split, without any great problems?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't go, but I think that was possible, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: And was there medical care and attention available? Were doctors working?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: Was it all free of charge or did you have to pay?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't think we had to pay.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: You didn't have to pay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: And now when people would go to Split for an examination of any kind, did they have to pay the hospital fees there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I really can't say. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: Did you hear anybody complain when they went to Split that they had to pay for their hospital fees?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I didn't hear of anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: I'd just like to show a map, map 29, to the witness before my time is up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam, Mr. Praljak has just asked you a series of questions and I have a question myself, a follow-up question. In your written statement, you explain that -- how in your village you could see Croatian television. Now, I'd like to know why you weren't receiving Sarajevo television. Could you explain that? Why couldn't you watch Sarajevo television?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because we didn't receive a signal, any signal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No signals. Right. So was that due to the configuration of the terrain or was there no relay station, or maybe the -- or you couldn't watch Sarajevo television even in previous years?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We could watch Sarajevo television before, but we couldn't at that time, and I don't know why. I don't know the reason. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] May I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you said that before you received the signal and could watch Sarajevo television, afterwards you couldn't because there was no signal; is that right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right. We received a signal before but not at that time, and I don't know why. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: Madam, you know that there was a general relay station put up at Velez for the region?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Everybody knows that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: And you could see the relay station and you were able to see, I'm sure, that in 1992, the Serbs destroyed it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: So it was this relay station that catered to the entire area and when that was destroyed, there was no further possibility of watching Sarajevo television; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd now like to have a look at the following document which is map 29, please, page 30 of the map. On e-court, it is P 09276. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] May I have the usher's assistance, please, and could she take the map to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, you have not received a copy of this map, that folder, because it was a map and it exists on e-court. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: Madam, I have drawn up a map where you can see the river Neretva and Pocitelj, and could you just mark on that map where the crossings were. Sevas Polje, crossing at Sevas Polje, and Pocitelj. Just put crosses by those two places, please. Larger, so we can see them better.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: And put a 1. That's Sevas Polje. Put number 1. Oh, that's Pocitelj. Right. So put number 1 by Pocitelj. At Sevas Polje, a little further up, you can put a number 2 there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: And put today's date there, too, and your signature, please. We have to follow procedure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And put a CG as well, the initials CG. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: And the date, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Registrar, may we have an IC number for that, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be IC number 118. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] I've almost finish.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: Can you just tell me one more thing? Throughout the spring of 1992 and the first half of 1993, despite the war that was being waged, the life of civilians, both the displaced persons and everybody, was relatively tolerable and that Croats and Muslims were -- not only were they in the army together but the whole atmosphere was tolerant if we don't count the exceptions to the -- this example. Would that be the general rule?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: You also say -- you said something that when we arrived at the lines at Stolac facing the Serbs, because they were far mightier, there was a lull there, and then you say, "According to an agreement with the Croats." Do you think there was an agreement between the Croats and Serbs to calm the situation down or was that the rumour going round?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was the rumour going round, but since we experienced the shelling by the Serbs, we realised that they were very strong and that it was very difficult to budge them, to get them away from that territory.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: But we nonetheless held the line?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: Now, for the -- do you know that for the Virgin Mary holiday, that in Herzegovina and with the Catholics is very celebrated, based on the 15th of August and in 1992, there was a large-scale offensive with Serb tanks against Stolac? Have you heard of that offensive of theirs? And we barely survived. Just say yes or no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't confirm this with any certainty.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: Well, thank you, Witness, for your answers. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] That completes my examination. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We're going to take our break and we'll have one hour left afterwards for the remaining four Defence teams. I'd like to give this document back to the registrar. It is Mr. Praljak's document with an IC number. And we reconvene at 5 minutes past 4.00. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Is it Counsel Nozica next? Yes, Ms. Egels.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: Sorry. Just for the record, Your Honour, I believe there is a little mistake. During the examination, the cross-examination by Mr. Praljak, on page 38, lines 7 and 8, he referred to a map, map number 29, that he showed to the witness being P 9270. The map that was shown to the witness is not map 29. It seems that it is an amalgamation of two maps, map 28 and 29. So for the record, what has been marked and now given the number IC 110 is not map 29. No, 118, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: While we're correcting the record, I think I noticed that when the witness dated the map put to her by Mr. Praljak, in fact, she put yesterday's date. That probably just ought to be corrected.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes, I agree. It is -- the maps Mr. Praljak used are actually the copies of two pages from the Prosecutor's evidence, and since the Prosecution was kind enough to prepare that document, I think that having that document changed into the IC, I think that there should not be any problem. But if needed, we can produce the same maps which the Prosecution actually used for that chart from the book where they took it as well. Yes. Exactly, Your Honour. Thank you for showing me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The important thing is to have 1 and 2 that was marked, the crossing points across the river. The rest is less important. Yes, Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with the Court's permission, I would like publicly to apologise to my learned friend of the Prosecution. My remark that her question in relation to an exhibit -- well, what I said was unfounded because, yes, my colleague did indeed mention civilian authorities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Ms. Nozica, you have 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. For the record, I would like to inform the Trial Chamber, very precisely, that I have my own 15 minutes, seven minutes from Mr. Coric's Defence and seven minutes from Mr. Pusic's Defence, which makes 28 minutes in all for the record. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Our legal advisor will do the calculations. It's getting a bit complicated now.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. It's no less complicated for me, but I'll try and get through my questions before the allotted time.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, madam.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I have placed a pink folder next to you. You needn't look at it now, but when I come to show you two documents, you will find those documents in that binder. And we're going to start off with the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we move into private session because I want to ask the something that might disclose her identity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Madam, tell me, do you know that on the 30th of June, 1993, the BH army, in cooperation with part of the HVO members who were Muslims, of Muslim ethnicity, attacked and took control of the so-called North Camp in Mostar and the Tihomir Misic barracks, and the entire territory of Bijelo Polje north of Mostar when certain -- a certain number of HVO members were killed and some civilians detained who happened to be in the area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I heard about most of it. Not about everything, but most of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: So we can take it that you knew of these events, did you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You also go on to say in your statement, that after that day, that is to say the 30th of June, 1993, your husband, together with the other fugitives from Kapa's unit, as you say, and with a number of locals, took to the forests and hid there; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Would it be correct to conclude, in view of what you say on page 7 of your statement, it is page 7 of the B/C/S and paragraph 4 in the English, that on that territory at that time, and we're talking about the 13th of July until the end of month, there were about 300 members of the BH army or, rather, that that group contained about 300 men?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. But it wasn't only at Bivolje Brdo. It was the entire area of Dubravska Visoravan.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I see, those 300 were all there. Now, how was that whole group armed? Do you know anything about Kapa's unit, whether they had any weapons or --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All I can tell you is whether my husband had any arms. I can't tell you about the rest, whether they did or did not.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I'm speaking slowly for the record, because everything you and I say has to be recorded. Can we then say that it is true and correct that your husband had an automatic rifle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we can say that.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: In your statement, in several places, you say that the members of the HVO came by to ask you where your husbands were and that they were looking for weapons mostly; is that right? Hidden weapons in the houses.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I'd like us to go back into private session, because I have to go into some details now.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Do you know that -- may I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's move into open session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Madam, do you have any information about this group? Do you know that this group, and your husband was in it, and you actively helped him, and there are many details about that in your statement, do you know that on the 13th of July, this group was involved in sabotage action against the HVO? This group or some other group that was on the Dubrava plateau, as you say. Are you aware of any sabotage committed against the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I heard about such sabotage action but I don't know who was involved in the sabotage. I wasn't there. I didn't see it. But later, when I spoke to my husband, I found out that, in fact, on the 14th, he was already in Blagaj. But I have heard about that sabotage and about acts of sabotage being committed.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: In your statement you described the Croatian soldiers who were detained in a garage. There was Mujo Sose halfway between the hamlet of Lokva and Vitina. At that point in time, I think it was on the 13th of July, according to your statement -- well, at that time, was there any fighting between the ABiH and the HVO? And what happened? Could that be described as a sabotage action carried out by those in the area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you. We heard the sounds of -- the sound of firing and explosions, but in the area that we were actually in, we didn't see a single soldier at that time, at the time that I saw those prisoners. I think they were prisoners because they were imprisoned. They were kept behind locked doors. But at that time and in that area, there was no fighting. You could only hear explosions in the distance.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: But you don't know the circumstances under which they were imprisoned. You don't know whether a group of inhabitants from your village, from the surrounding villages, or members of the ABiH had come and imprisoned them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I'd like to remind you about part of your statement in which you describe the event, an event that appears to be a sabotage action, in my opinion. I'd like to refer you to page 8. And it's also page 8 in the English version of your statement, the penultimate passage. And you say, "I was surprised that HVO soldiers could have been taken prisoner when they occupied the village, as if it was their place. I thought that the men hiding in the woods had probably managed to take some prisoners. I didn't see anyone else in the area who could have done that." And just wait briefly before you answer. Is that what you said in your statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Madam, from the 1st and up until the 13th, we saw only HVO members with our own eyes. That's why I said that they had quite simply taken over the village. But the men who had fled, well, they were in the woods. But during that period, there were only HVO soldiers walking around the village, and they would enter houses and maltreat people. That's why I said that.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Very well, madam. But there were Croatian soldiers who were imprisoned there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: By Muslims. They had been imprisoned by Muslims.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I suppose they didn't imprison themselves.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Very well. That's all I wanted to ask you about. Thank you. You said that you had heard about sabotage actions. I'd like to ask you whether you heard about anything else. Did you hear about the killing of the ambulance driver and the wounding of a nurse on the 13th of July? And you described quite a lot of events on that day. This took place in Domanovici on the road to Capljina. It's fairly close to your village. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Let's have a look at something that might refresh your memory. Let's have a look at document 2D 00276. It's the first document that you have. While waiting for it to appear on the screen, and the Judges have the document, too, I'll move on. It's dated the 14th of July, the health sectors, Defence department, and it states the following: "Yesterday in Domanovici, on the road to Capljina, while transporting wounded, there was an ambush and a burst of fire was opened as a result of which Franjo Boskovic, the ambulance driver, was killed. And as a result of that same burst of fire, the nurse, Mijatovic Vesna, was seriously wounded." I haven't got much time. I have another important document under -- I'll read out the next page. "The late Franjo, up until yesterday and from the beginning of the war, would save people in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina regardless of their ethnicity or religion. He was killed by members of the MOS yesterday." Have you heard anything about this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And you never heard about this afterwards either?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: May I? When we were taken to the Silos, well, the soldiers showed us the road that had been damaged beneath the cemetery in Domanovici, and they said, "You done even know who did this." And that's when we found out about this act of sabotage in Domanovici, if that's where it was. Otherwise, I know nothing about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Very well. Let's have a look at the next document, P 08648. And listen to my question while we're waiting for the document to come up on the screen. Have you heard about someone being killed or, rather, 23 HVO members being killed and about 10 being wounded in the Gubavica sector, which isn't far from your house? Isn't that correct? In fact, it was on the 15th of July, 1993, at the Dubrava plateau. On that day, on the 16th of July, you were in Gradina, and you were in Becir Boskailo's house for about eight days. So during that period, did you hear anything about this act of sabotage?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I heard that soldiers had been killed, but I didn't see anything and I wasn't there, but I heard about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: This event in which these soldiers were killed was quite important. A lot of people suffered. It was the day of the dead in Capljina on that day. Did you hear anything about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Since this document has to do with what you have said in your statement, I'd like to have a look at it together with you. At the beginning, on the first page -- well, the document is dated the 8th of February, 1996, but it mentions the sabotage in the Gubavica sector, the Dubrava plateau, and the result of the act of sabotage was that there were 23 dead and 10 wounded. Then there was this event on the 15th of July, 1993, and as I have said, there were 23 men killed and 10 wounded. This could have been prevented if everyone had acted responsibly, if everybody had performed their duties. The intelligence service informed their superiors in written form on two occasions and -- on the 3rd of July and just before the event itself on the 11th of July, 1993. I will just read out the next paragraph: "The intelligence service with Bruno Krvavac, the chief at its at its head, carried out operative work and reconnaissance and found out that the ABiH was planning sabotage terrorist action in that area in cooperation with ABiH members who had remained in the Dubrava area." Let's have a look at the next page of the document. It's a Prosecution document. First, we have an intelligence record. It was mentioned in the previous document. It's dated the 11th of July. Have a look at the original, although we have it on the screen now. Let's have a look at it together. Item 1 -- or, in fact it says: "Through analysis of intelligence received from intelligence sources, we have obtained the following information: Three groups of a total of 150 men have been spotted in the forest above Satorova Gomila in the area towards Stanojevici. Most of them are between 25 and 30 years of age. All members of this group have automatic infantry weapons, and they also have a certain number of Zolja hand-held rocket launchers and rocket-propelled grenades." You said your husband had an automatic rifle. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: In your statement, you also said that certain individuals, whose names I won't mention since we are in open session, you also said that some of his comrades had automatic rifles. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now let's have a look at item 7. Item 7: "The basic communication between the groups on the run is through a courier, but there's also a possibility that someone or more of them have wireless equipment." On page 7 -- on page 7, the last paragraph in the English version, you said that you had provided batteries for radios to some of the -- to one of the men who came, who was with your husband, because he had problems communicating with Buna. I won't mention his name since we are in open session. Isn't that correct though?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He wasn't with my husband. He came and we went to the shelter which was far away from my house. He came from the other part of the village. Mine husband was hiding in the vicinity of our house then.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Could we agree that there were several groups, as it says here, and they weren't all at the same location? He was at another location, as you say. He wasn't at the same location as your husband.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He came from another direction. All I know is where my husband was.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Did he ask for a battery, because he said he had interference and he wanted to be able to communicate with Buna?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he said something like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Who was at Buna at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Very well. Let's have a look at item 9. "On the basis of what has been said, there's the possibility of maintaining contact between the members of the group and majority of the armija forces in Blagaj and Mostar area, and there's also the possibility of organising and synchronising the action of these individuals." Item 10: "Certain group commanders insist on sabotage and terrorist acts and activities." This document is dated the 11th of July and it corresponds to what you said you knew about. You heard about certain terrorists and sabotage groups. Isn't that correct? Or, rather, you heard about such activities.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I heard something about that but never from my husband. He never gave me an answer to anything like that, either positive or negative.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Well, I can understand why he didn't do that, but you heard not from your husband but, as you said, from others that this kind of thing happened. Now, let's take a look at the next document, the 3rd of July. Once again, it is an intelligence report. So let's skip the first point and focus on the second bullet point. It says: "There is realistic possibility for group and individual sabotage and intelligence activities, and we especially would like to focus on the individuals and groups aimed at linking up, organising themselves with the ultimate intention of breaking through in the direction of the BH army units in the area around Blagaj." Now, you say something about that in your own statement. Do you know whether at that time you were aware of the fact that certain people from the military circles of Mostar wanted to meet this group, and do you know if there were any initiatives in that regard or whether this linking up actually happened? Did they manage to link up with the Mostar people with these small groups which together, as you say, made up the 300 resistance fighters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I've already told you, I heard something about that but I didn't get a definite answer from anybody as to whether that was true or not, so I can't really answer your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Well, I'll end there with my last question. On page 7 of your statement you said, and I'll read it out to you. Take a look at page 7, please. It says: "My husband" -- you say, "While I was going to take some stores to my husband, I heard rumours that somebody would arrive from Mostar to have a meeting with a group of people who were hiding in the woods and help them to set up the defence lines towards Rude near the bauxite mine." Now, I'm interested in this next paragraph. It says: "My husband never confirm the rumour to me, but I know that will he was involved with the group in an operation coordinated with the villagers in the region. In all, there were about 300 resistance fighters, but I can't tell you any more than that." Now, my question is this: What was your husband involved in together with the other co-fighters? So this whole group, not only your husband, but what did you have in mind when you say, "But I know that he was involved in the operation"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what it was about and what was going on, but as he was with them and talked to them and moved around in the forest with them, naturally he was involved. That's how I concluded that he knew about something. But otherwise, I didn't have any special indicators. Since he was with them, he wasn't an exception. He must have been with them in whatever they were about.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now, you took a fairly active role, and I'm not criticising you for that, I'm just stating it as a fact, but what was your role in actual fact? What did you think you were doing when you were taking weapons that had been dug into the ground? You dug them up. You played a very active role in bringing in information, news, resources, equipment. What was that group preparing to do? Was it preparing to continue fighting the Serbs, or was it preparing to fight the Croats? What would you say in view of all of the things that you have said in your statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't exactly what they were getting ready for, but I thought they were getting ready to break through to free territory and escape. That's what I thought. I wasn't thinking of any sabotage, killing, or the like. All I thought was, quite simply, that they wanted to gather together and then break through together to go to Blagaj, Mostar, or further on.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: But nevertheless, as we've seen from the documents that I showed you, and on the basis of your own knowledge, throughout that time, some sabotage activities were going on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You confirmed a moment ago that you had heard about some of them.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I heard about them later on, not at that actual point in time.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Next Defence counsel. Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Witness, when your husband was home on the night of the 30th of June, 1993, you say that he was on leave. How long was he on leave for as planned at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think he was supposed to go back in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
